summary: Describes NEC's Simple Middlebox Configuration protocol, version 3.0, for controlling middleboxes such as firewalls and network address translators. It implements the semantics from the Middlebox Communications framework in RFC 3989 and, unlike earlier experimental versions, uses binary messages. This is an experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: Some network boxes act like door guards. SIMCO lets a program send a guard short instructions, such as who may come through, using compact machine-friendly messages.

questions: how to configure a firewall or nat remotely
subtitle: A compact binary protocol that lets applications ask firewalls and NATs to open pinholes and create address bindings.

tldr.problem: Firewalls and network address translators (NATs) get in the way of traffic such as peer-to-peer applications that use dynamically negotiated UDP or TCP ports, and small middleboxes cannot afford heavy text-based protocols.
tldr.mechanism: SIMCO 3.0 lets an agent open a session to a middlebox over a reliable transport such as TCP and send binary type-length-value messages to reserve, enable, change and disable policy rules, following the MIDCOM semantics of RFC 3989.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental protocol, not a candidate for any Internet Standard, and an IESG note urges caution before implementing or deploying it. It has since been updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 4540 is an Experimental protocol and has been updated by RFC 8996. Its own IESG note says it is not a candidate for any level of Internet Standard.

sections.title: Controlling Middleboxes
sections.content:
The Simple Middlebox Configuration (SIMCO) protocol controls firewalls and network address translators. These are middleboxes: devices on the datagram path that do more than just IP routing. They can block streams that use dynamically negotiated UDP or TCP port numbers, as many peer-to-peer applications do.

SIMCO lets applications talk to the middleboxes on the path and request a dynamic configuration so datagram streams can pass. Applications can request pinholes at firewalls and address bindings at NATs. The semantics come from RFC 3989, and this document gives the concrete protocol.

Earlier experimental versions used simple ASCII encodings. Version 3.0 uses a binary encoding because text needs more resources to generate and parse. The authors give two reasons: session setup times are critical for applications such as IP telephony, and many middleboxes are small, low-cost devices.
sections.plainLanguage: A program can ask the guard at the network door to let a particular friend in. SIMCO is the short, quick way to ask.

sections.title: MIDCOM Semantics and Sessions
sections.content:
SIMCO 3 is fully compliant with the MIDCOM protocol semantics of RFC 3989. It supports all mandatory transactions but does not implement the optional group transactions. It adds one transaction of its own, Policy Disable Rule (PDR), which security functions such as intrusion detection can use to block a kind of traffic. PDRs have priority over Policy Enable Rules (PERs): when a PDR is established, all conflicting PERs are terminated, and no new conflicting PER can be set up until the PDR ends. Support for PDR is optional.

A session has two parties, an agent representing one or more applications and a middlebox. The agent initiates the session. An agent may talk to several middleboxes, one session per middlebox, and a middlebox may serve several agents, one session per agent.

Sessions must run over a reliable transport. Implementations must support TCP, and when using TCP a middlebox must wait for agents to connect on port 7626, assigned by IANA. The session may be secured with IPsec or TLS for authentication, message integrity and confidentiality.
sections.plainLanguage: A helper program (the agent) calls a guard (the middlebox) and keeps one phone line open to each guard it works with.

sections.title: Message Headers and Attributes
sections.content:
Every SIMCO message is Type-Length-Value (TLV) encoded in big endian binary. A message starts with a 64-bit header holding the basic type, a sub-type, the message length (excluding the header, in octets) and a transaction identifier (TID). The rest, the payload, holds zero or more TLV attributes, each starting with a 16-bit type and a 16-bit length.

The basic type is a request (0x01), positive reply (0x02), negative reply (0x03) or notification (0x04). Messages from the agent are always requests. The sub-type then says what the message is about, for example session establishment (SE, 0x01), policy reserve rule (PRR, 0x11) or policy enable rule (PER, 0x12).

The agent picks a TID that it never reuses in two requests in the same session, and replies carry the TID of their request. The middlebox does the same for notifications. Defined attributes include the protocol version (major 3, minor 0 for this document), authentication challenge and token (up to 4096 octets), middlebox capabilities, policy rule identifier, group identifier, policy rule lifetime, policy rule owner (up to 255 octets), address tuple, and PRR and PER parameter sets.

The capabilities attribute carries an MB type bit field: 0x80 packet filter firewall, 0x40 network address translator, 0x10 PDR support, and for NATs 0x01 port translation, 0x02 protocol translation and 0x04 twice NAT. A NAPT with packet filter and PDR support has the value 0xD1.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message starts with a small label that says what kind of note it is and how long it is, and then comes the list of details.

sections.title: Sessions and Policy Rules
sections.content:
Each session has a state machine. All sessions start CLOSED. A successful SE transaction moves a session to NOAUTH or straight to OPEN, and from NOAUTH a successful SA (session authentication) moves it to OPEN. A failed SA returns it to CLOSED. A successful ST (session termination) or an AST notification (asynchronous session termination) closes a NOAUTH or OPEN session. OPEN is the only state in which the middlebox accepts requests other than SE, SA and ST.

Policy rules have their own state machine per policy rule identifier (PID). A PRR request makes a RESERVED rule, a PER request makes an ENABLED rule, and PEA enables a reserved rule. A PLC request changes the lifetime, and a lifetime of zero deletes the rule. An ARE notification reports an asynchronous policy rule event.

Incoming messages go through format checks first. If the header check fails, the middlebox sends a BFM notification, and if a session is already established it also sends AST and closes the connection. If it waits 60 seconds without receiving more octets of a message, it does the same. Wrong basic types and sub-types, and badly formed requests, get negative replies such as 0x0310, 0x0311 and 0x0312.
sections.plainLanguage: Before anyone can give orders, they must first say hello, and maybe prove who they are. Only then can they ask the guard to hold a spot or let someone in.

sections.title: Threats and IPsec
sections.content:
Letting an outside entity configure a firewall looks counterproductive at first, since an attacker who could do so might open the firewall for his own traffic. The RFC lists four threats: a man-in-the-middle attack that alters messages, changing message content, replaying earlier messages, and wiretapping, where a configured policy rule with too broad a wildcard is reused by other hosts.

SIMCO can rely on IPsec in transport mode, using the authentication header (AH) against content changes and replaying and the encapsulating security payload (ESP) to prevent wiretapping. The agent and middlebox addresses, TCP and port numbers should be pre-configured, only packets from the pre-configured addresses should be accepted, and keys are pre-configured at each side. For replay protection, a key management system is recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: If a stranger could talk to the guard, they could tell it to open the gates. So the calls must be locked and signed so only the right helper can give orders.

sections.title: Experimental Status and UNSAF
sections.content:
An IESG note says the content was considered by the IETF at one time and that this RFC is not a candidate for any level of Internet Standard. The IETF disclaims knowledge of its fitness for any purpose, and publication was not based on IETF review of security, congestion control or interaction with deployed protocols. Readers should exercise caution in evaluating it for implementation and deployment.

The document also addresses the IAB's UNSAF considerations. It argues that MIDCOM is not a short-term work-around like STUN-style approaches but a long-term solution, because the full control of addresses and ports at the middlebox sits with the SIMCO server and endpoints are not involved in allocating or deleting them.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF says: this is an experiment, so be careful before building it into anything important.

fields.name: Basic Type
fields.desc: Request, positive reply, negative reply or notification.

fields.name: Sub-Type
fields.desc: Further information within the basic type.

fields.name: Message Length
fields.desc: Length of the message in octets, excluding the SIMCO header.

fields.name: Transaction Identifier (TID)
fields.desc: Identifies the transaction; replies repeat the request's TID.
